name: Self-Reflection in LLM Agents: Effects on Problem-Solving Performance
authors: Matthew Renze, Erhan Guven (Johns Hopkins University)
venue: IEEE 2024 2nd International Conference on Foundation and Large Language Models (FLLM), pp. 516-525 (DOI 10.1109/FLLM63129.2024.10852426); first released as arXiv preprint 2405.06682
code_url: https://github.com/matthewrenze/self-reflection (BSD-2-Clause; includes all code, exams, reflections, dialogs, results)
reflection_type: verbal-self-critique (eight prompt-engineered self-reflection variants: Retry, Keywords, Advice, Explanation, Instructions, Solution, Composite, Unredacted) over the agent's own chain-of-thought
feedback_source: self-generated natural-language reflection conditioned on a ground-truth-oracle signal: the agent is told its first answer was wrong and is given the correct answer to reflect on (answer labels/descriptions then redacted to prevent direct leakage, except for the Unredacted upper-bound agent)
iteration_structure: episodic-retry-with-reset: single reflection + single re-answer of each previously-incorrect question (implemented as 4 batch phases representing virtual multi-step agents); not multi-round iterative refinement
reflection_object: reasoning chain / output content — the agent reflects on its own chain-of-thought and incorrect solution, producing verbal artifacts (error keywords, explanation of the mistake, step-by-step solution, ordered instructions, general advice) that are injected into the re-answer prompt context; no weights, code, or persistent skill library are modified
reward_or_critic_model: self-as-judge for generating the reflection text, but the improvement signal is supplied by a ground-truth-oracle (the known correct answer provided during the reflection step); no trained reward or critic model
distillation_target: prompt — reflections are distilled into natural-language guidance (keywords/advice/explanation/instructions/solution) injected back into the re-answer prompt; they are not persisted into long-term memory, weights, or a reusable skill library in this study (authors note RAG-based memory as future work)
emergent_vs_engineered: prompt/scaffold-engineered: each of the eight reflection types is produced via hand-designed prompt templates (Reflexion/Self-Refine lineage); reflection is not RL-emergent
memory_type: short-term/scratchpad — the generated self-reflection text is held only within the re-answer prompt for the same question; no persistent episodic store
memory_persistence: within-episode (reflection applied only to the same question that was failed; no cross-task transfer; authors flag cross-problem retrieval/RAG memory as future work)
memory_curation_mechanism: n/a — single-use reflection text per question with answer redaction; no accumulation or curation of a memory bank
error_localization_granularity: response-level / holistic outcome-level: the agent knows only that its final MCQA answer was incorrect (binary correct/incorrect outcome) and reflects on the whole solution; no step-level or token-level error localization
intra_task_vs_inter_task: intra-task: reflection is used to re-answer the exact same failed question, not to transfer experience across different tasks (Self-Refine-like within-question correction rather than Reflexion-style cross-episode transfer)
failure_recovery_vs_avoidance: post-hoc-revision: the agent revises its answer to the same question after being told it was wrong; not mid-trajectory recovery and not next-episode avoidance
task_domains: QA/reasoning (multiple-choice question answering) spanning science, math, common-sense reasoning, logic, law/analytic reasoning, medicine, English
benchmarks: 1,000-question multi-domain MCQA exam (100 randomly sampled questions from each of 10 source sets): ARC Challenge, AGIEval subsets (AQUA-RAT, LogiQA, LSAT-AR, LSAT-LR, LSAT-RC, SAT-English, SAT-Math), HellaSwag, MedMCQA
headline_result: Self-reflection significantly improved accuracy for every reflection type across all 9 LLMs (McNemar test, p<0.001). Example (GPT-4): baseline 0.786 to Composite 0.932 (+0.146); Solution 0.925 (+0.139); Unredacted upper bound 0.971 (+0.185).
baselines: Non-reflecting Baseline agent (same prompt-engineering: domain expertise, CoT, conciseness, few-shot, temperature 0.0) as control/lower bound; the Unredacted agent (reflection with correct answer not redacted) serves as upper bound
gains_vs_baseline: Information-richer reflections beat information-poorer ones. GPT-4 deltas vs baseline (0.786): Retry +0.041, Keywords +0.046, Advice +0.054, Instructions +0.063, Explanation +0.090, Solution +0.139, Composite +0.146, Unredacted +0.185. Largest per-exam gain on LSAT-AR (GPT-4 0.33->0.76 with Solution). Llama 2 70B improved baseline 0.376->0.672 (Composite); GPT-3.5 0.596->0.827; Claude 3 Opus 0.792->0.947.
compute_cost_profile: Roughly 2-3x inference passes per failed item versus single-pass baseline: one baseline answer pass, one reflection-generation pass, and one re-answer pass for each incorrectly answered question (re-answering only the failed subset, not all 1,000, to save cost); no training cost (training-free)
known_limitations: (1) Single-step problems only — does not demonstrate multi-step/long-horizon agent value; (2) API content-safety errors may add <1% error generally, up to ~2.8% for Gemini 1.0 Pro and Mistral Large; (3) ceiling/compression effect as top LLMs exceed 90% on easy exams, masking true gains; (4) results skewed by the single hard LSAT-AR exam which benefited most; reflection is applied only to re-answer the identical question (no cross-problem generalization or external memory tested).
oracle_or_external_feedback_dependency: oracle-label/ground-truth: the self-reflection is generated only AFTER the agent is given the correct answer as an external feedback signal. Even with answer labels/descriptions redacted, the Explanation/Instructions/Solution/Composite agents indirectly leak the correct answer through reflection content. This is the discriminating caveat — gains are not from intrinsic self-verification but from reflecting against a known correct answer.
self_correction_efficacy: requires-oracle: net-positive and statistically significant, but gains are conditioned on knowing the correct answer at reflection time; the study does not demonstrate label-free intrinsic self-correction (consistent with Huang et al. 2023 'LLMs cannot self-correct reasoning yet', which the authors cite)
calibration_effect: not-measured — the paper reports accuracy and McNemar significance only; no calibration/confidence or overconfidence ('reasoning tax') analysis. Anecdotally the Retry agent improved purely from knowing it was previously wrong, but calibration is not quantified.
failure_attribution_capability: n/a — not a failure-attribution study; the Keywords agent does produce a coarse self-classification of error types (general-to-specific keywords) but there is no formal failure-mode taxonomy or responsible-agent/step attribution
failure_mode_addressed: Targets superficial/uninformative self-reflection by decomposing reflection into eight information-content levels and showing richer feedback (Solution/Explanation/Instructions) yields larger gains; also motivated by avoiding repeated-mistake error-loops where agents get stuck repeating the same error
dataset_or_benchmark_released: Yes — the curated 1,000-question multi-domain MCQA exam plus all reflections, dialogs, per-question details, logs, and results CSVs released on GitHub (matthewrenze/self-reflection, BSD-2-Clause)
builds_on: Reflexion (Shinn et al. 2023); Self-Refine (Madaan et al. 2023); ReAct (Yao et al. 2022); CoT prompting (Wei et al. 2022; Kojima et al. 2022); the self-correction survey of Pan et al. 2023; the authors' own prior work on concise CoT (Renze & Guven 2024) and sampling temperature (Renze & Guven 2024); contrasts with Huang et al. 2023 and Tyen et al. 2023 on the limits of intrinsic self-correction
extended_by_or_inspired: Cited by ~18 papers (Semantic Scholar) including 'Problem-Solving in Language Model Networks' (Regan, Gournail & Oka, arXiv 2406.12374, 2024) which extends self-reflection vs. interconnectedness in multi-agent debate networks; broadly cited in LLM metacognition / self-reflection and agent-self-correction follow-up work
citation_count: 18 (Semantic Scholar, paperId 92f81cd548ae953b7416fc6db6d5602f7a9d9a39, as of mid-2025; GitHub repo ~94 stars)
reasoning_model_native: No — the study predates and does not target o1/R1-style reasoning models with built-in reflection; it evaluates 2023-2024 chat LLMs (GPT-4, GPT-3.5, Claude 3 Opus, Gemini 1.0/1.5 Pro, Llama 2 7B/70B, Command R+, Mistral Large) where reflection is externally prompt-induced rather than RL-emergent
on_policy_distillation_link: Weak/indirect — reflections are distilled only into the in-context re-answer prompt (no on-policy rollout distillation into weights or a skill library); relevant to OPD only as a training-free verbal analogue, with the explicit caveat that the improvement signal comes from a ground-truth oracle rather than on-policy self-generated correctness
sample_efficiency: One reflection + one re-answer per failed question reaches the reported gains (single-iteration, no multi-trial search); reflection generated and applied only to previously-incorrect items
